title: The Sleeping Harvest
premise: Lena Lockridge, a hospice nurse who has spent fifteen years hearing the dying count backwards toward something no one names, inherits their estranged grandmother's farmhouse and discovers the family fortune was built on a bargain: each generation feeds the harvest moon one remembered life in exchange for prosperity. The mirrors lag because the house is already rehearsing Lena's death, replaying it one second behind reality. As the harvest moon rises, Lena must uncover which ancestor invited the thing in—and realize the only way out is to give it not their memory but the family's whole buried history, ending the inheritance at the cost of being forgotten by everyone who ever knew them.
about_author: August Whitlock is the pen name of a former night-shift caregiver who spent a decade collecting the strange things people say as they die. They write horror about houses that remember more than the people inside them.

chapters.title: The Counting Ward
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. At the hospice, Mr. Aldous counts backwards from thirty and dies smiling at the window. Lena notes it's the fourth patient this month to count toward the same date: the harvest moon. Emotional beat: dread disguised as professional detachment.

chapters.title: Letters from a Dead Woman
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. A lawyer's letter reveals grandmother Edith Lockridge left Lena the farmhouse—despite fifteen years of silence. The letter includes one instruction: 'Don't sleep past midnight on the last night of September.' Beat: uneasy curiosity.

chapters.title: The House That Waits
chapters.summary: Lena arrives at the farmhouse, finding every clock stopped at 11:58 and dust undisturbed except fresh footprints leading upstairs. POV shifts briefly to the house itself in a chilling interlude. Beat: wrongness beneath welcome.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Washing up, Lena notices their reflection blinks after they do. Testing it with a metronome confirms it: every mirror lags exactly one second. Beat: rationalization cracking against evidence.

chapters.title: Edith's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the locked study, Lena finds a ledger listing generations of Lockridges with dates and sums—the money the family always had, matched to deaths. The final page reserves a blank line dated for the coming harvest moon. Beat: inheritance revealed as debt.

chapters.title: The Neighbor Who Knows
chapters.summary: Ruth Calloway, an elderly neighbor, warns Lena off the property but slips when she mentions 'the second Lena.' She was Edith's friend once, before Edith stopped speaking to her. Beat: the first ally, and the first confirmation Lena isn't crazy.

chapters.title: What the Dying Know
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Lena's POV, fifteen years earlier: the first time Lena heard a patient counting backwards, and how they learned to stop listening. Interwoven with present-day realization that the counting patients all shared the Lockridge surname in their charts. Beat: guilt over years of willful blindness.

chapters.title: The Second Lena
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. In the hall mirror, the reflection moves independently for three full seconds—smiling, mouthing words. Lip-reading yields two syllables: 'stay here.' Beat: terror turning personal; the house wants a replacement.

chapters.title: Root Cellar Sermons
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth breaks into her own suppressed memories: as girls, she and Edith witnessed Edith's father feeding something in the root cellar—a bundle of letters, photographs, a wedding dress, burned under the moon while he recited names. Beat: the bargain's mechanics revealed through witness.

chapters.title: Memory Is Currency
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Researching the ledger against county records, Lena finds every prosperous Lockridge year followed a fire or disappearance, and every family member died unable to recognize their own portraits. The thing doesn't take lives—it takes the memory of them. Beat: understanding the true price.

chapters.title: Invitation
chapters.summary: The house's POV, second person. It remembers the night in 1893 when the first Lockridge, starving, read aloud from a book found in the collapsed mine and asked the dark for a harvest that never fails. It has been fed ever since. Beat: mythic dread; the origin.

chapters.title: Fifteen Years of Noise
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. The noises Lena spent fifteen years explaining—pipes, raccoons, settling timber—replay in the farmhouse, identical, and Lena finally admits they were never explanations. The reflection now waits at windows. Beat: collapse of denial; grief for the self who coped.

chapters.title: Ruth's Confession
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth admits she helped Edith prepare a substitute offering forty years ago—an unnamed orphan's belongings—and has been running from it since. She gives Lena Edith's final letter, unopened. Beat: complicity, and the weight of survival.

chapters.title: Edith's Last Letter
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Edith's letter explains she refused to feed it this year, choosing to die forgotten rather than pass the debt down—but the thing accepted Lena's name anyway, written long ago in the ledger by Lena's own mother. Beat: betrayal; the inheritance was signed in Lena's blood line.

chapters.title: The Moon Rises Early
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. The harvest moon appears a night ahead of schedule; clocks all jump to 11:58. The reflection stops mimicking entirely and begins cleaning the house, preparing it. Beat: point of no return; siege begins.

chapters.title: Holding Out Until Sunrise
chapters.summary: Lena and Ruth barricade the kitchen as the house rearranges itself around them, doors opening onto 1893, onto the hospice, onto Lena's own childhood. The counting starts outside the walls—dozens of voices, backwards. Beat: endurance horror; loyalty under pressure.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV, dying memories surfacing: the thing in the mine wasn't summoned—it was buried there by miners who starved it, and the Lockridges' crime was waking it and teaching it to eat memory instead of flesh. Beat: the monster reframed as something wronged into hunger.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. At midnight the reflection steps out of the mirror wearing Lena's face and offers the old deal: prosperity, longevity, one small forgetting per generation. It shows Lena their mother, alive somewhere, having paid with all memory of her daughter. Beat: temptation sharpened by longing.

chapters.title: A Different Payment
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Lena refuses and instead reads the entire ledger aloud to the thing—every name, every theft, every forgotten victim—forcing it to remember what it has eaten. Memory floods back into it like a meal of thorns. Beat: cleverness as weapon; turning the mechanism against itself.

chapters.title: Sunrise
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converge. The house convulses as the thing, gorged on its own stolen history, drags the mirrors, the ledger, and the reflection down into the floor. Ruth dies at dawn holding Lena's hand, whispering Lena's name so someone will have said it. Beat: costly victory.

chapters.title: Nobody's Grandchild
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, weeks later. The price holds: no one remembers Lena—not the hospice, not the town. Lena keeps the farmhouse, mirrorless, and begins writing everything down so at least paper will know them. Beat: bittersweet freedom; identity preserved by choice, not recognition.

chapters.title: The Sleeping Harvest
chapters.summary: Final chapter, ambiguous coda. A new family moves in down the road; their child hears counting in the fields. Lena watches from the porch, ledger in hand, deciding whether the debt truly died or only sleeps. Last image: the unplanted field ripening overnight with no seed. Beat: quiet, unresolved dread.
